findings.title: Equal-order crypto providers are no longer a startup failure
findings.body: detectProvider now sorts CryptoProvider implementations by order() and, when more than one is present, logs the rest at debug and keeps foundProviders.get(0). DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200, so a classpath that contains more than one of them no longer hits the previous IllegalStateException. ServiceLoader order is classpath order, so a FIPS deployment that also has the default (or Elytron) provider can silently run non-FIPS crypto, or the reverse. Selection also instantiates every provider: FIPS1402Provider's constructor inserts BCFIPS/BCJSSE and may rewrite ssl.KeyManagerFactory.algorithm, and DefaultCryptoProvider registers non-FIPS BouncyCastle, and those JVM-wide side effects now remain in a running server instead of aborting startup. Tie on the highest order should still fail, and only a strictly lower order (such as AuthzClientCryptoProvider's 100) should be ignored.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JDK keystore provider
findings.body: CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider is contracted to return the BouncyCastle (or BCFIPS) provider. AuthzClientCryptoProvider instead returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which on a normal JDK is SUN, not BC. This provider is a ServiceLoader CryptoProvider and becomes the process-wide provider whenever it is the only one or wins order(). Callers that do Cipher/Signature.getInstance(alg, getBouncyCastleProvider()) or that register that provider under the name they expect to be "BC"/"BCFIPS" will use SUN or fail NoSuchProviderException. PKCS7Padding, BC named curves, and FIPS algorithm lookups break, and a non-null SUN provider also skips null fallbacks. This should throw like the other unimplemented methods, or return a real BC provider; it must not impersonate one.

findings.title: New abstract order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: order() was added as an abstract interface method with no default. keycloak-common is a published library, and CryptoProvider is a public SPI. Implementations compiled against the previous interface (downstream distributions, the separate keycloak-client tree, test fakes) will not compile, and old binaries will throw AbstractMethodError when ServiceLoader instantiates them during CryptoIntegration.init, which now runs from AuthzClient.create as well as server startup. A default method is required for compatibility. That default must be greater than AuthzClientCryptoProvider.order() (100); a default of 0 would let the incomplete authz-client provider outrank every legacy full provider that does not override order().

findings.title: ECDSA test never verifies signatures or curve-sized keys
findings.body: ECDSAAlgorithmTest builds one KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC") key (SunEC default P-256) and reuses it for ES256, ES384, and ES512. It only checks that asn1derToConcatenatedRS and concatenatedRSToASN1DER round-trip to the same byte array. ES384/ES512 therefore never see 48-byte or 66-byte R/S values (including the leading-0x00 high-bit case on P-521); those components are just zero-padded 32-byte integers, so both branches can be wrong for real curve sizes and the test still passes. Nothing calls Signature.verify on the re-encoded DER, so a DER encoding that this decoder accepts but Java rejects would stay green. There is also no test that ServiceLoader ordering prefers a higher order() over AuthzClientCryptoProvider, or that two providers with the same highest order are rejected.
